screens.title: Building for Different Platforms
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what it means to build a Unity project for different platforms and why that process is more than just clicking Build. Building compiles your scenes, assets, and scripts into an application package tailored for Windows, WebGL, Android, iOS, and other targets. You will see the key settings that control architecture, development instrumentation, and compression, and you’ll learn the extra toolchain steps required for mobile development. We’ll also walk through platform-specific code using conditional compilation so a single script can behave differently on desktop, mobile, and web. Understanding these stages helps you avoid common mistakes like missing scenes in the build list, wrong SDK paths, or forgetting to uncheck development builds for release. By the end of this chapter you should be able to prepare a simple project, switch targets in Build Settings, configure platform-specific options, and apply a testing plan to verify each build. Think about which platform you’ll ship first and what testing constraints you’ll need — that choice guides many of the configuration decisions you’ll make.

screens.title: What is the Build Process?
screens.narratorSegment: Building in Unity means transforming your project — scenes, assets, and scripts — into a platform-specific package that can run outside the Editor. The build pipeline performs several stages: it first collects the scenes listed in your build, then compiles managed code, processes and compresses assets for the target platform, and finally produces an executable bundle or web deployment package. A key point is that this is not a one-size-fits-all step. Different targets require different output formats, C P U architectures, and runtime support. For example, a Windows build produces an executable and a data folder, while WebGL produces JavaScript and WebAssembly files that run inside a browser. Understanding each stage helps you troubleshoot: missing scenes cause an app that launches without gameplay, incorrect scripting backends or A P I calls can fail at compile time, and mismatched SDK paths will stop mobile builds before compilation begins. A common misconception is that building only packages files — in reality it often reimports assets and can change compression or shader variants for a platform. Example: switching to WebGL can increase import time because textures and audio may be recompressed. Takeaway: treat the build as a staged compilation and test early with small scenes to confirm each stage works as expected. What small scene could you build first to validate your toolchain?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: The build is a staged compilation and packaging pipeline that outputs a runnable application for a chosen platform.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › What is the Build Process?
Definition

Build stages

  • Scene collection: use the Scenes In Build list to select startup content.
  • Code compilation: C# compiles to managed assemblies for the runtime.
  • Asset processing: textures, audio, and shaders are converted and compressed for the target.
  • Packaging: outputs an executable bundle or web files depending on the platform.
Misconception

Building is not just copying files. It often reimports and remaps assets, applies compression, and may strip or include platform-specific code paths.

Key Takeaway

Treat builds as a repeatable staged workflow. Validate each stage with a small scene before doing full game builds.

Concrete Example
Switch to WebGL
When you switch to WebGL, Unity may re-import textures with web-friendly compression and generate JavaScript and WebAssembly artifacts. These changes can increase import time and alter runtime memory usage.
Small-scene test
Create a minimal scene with your main menu and one level, add it to Scenes In Build, and build that first to confirm compilation, assets, and startup behavior.
Check Your Understanding

Why does Unity re-import assets when switching platforms and what practical step can you take to reduce surprises?

screens.title: Using File > Build Settings
screens.narratorSegment: File, Build Settings is the control center for choosing where your game will run. When you open it, you’ll see a list of available platforms such as PC, Mac & Linux Standalone, WebGL, Android, and iOS. Select a platform and click Switch Platform to make it active. Be aware that switching triggers a re-import for many assets, so it can take time. The Scenes In Build list determines which scenes Unity packages; always ensure your main menu or launcher scene is at index zero so startup ordering is predictable. If your build fails immediately after switching, check the Console for script compile errors and verify that platform-specific plugins are compatible. Practical tip: avoid frequent platform switching during active development — pick a primary target and only switch when you’re ready to test another platform. Example workflow: add your test scene to Scenes In Build, switch to Windows Standalone, choose x86_64, deselect Development Build for production, and then click Build to select a destination folder with write permissions. Watch for permission errors when saving into system-protected folders. What step would you add to a pre-build checklist to catch common errors?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Using File > Build Settings
Steps
  1. Open File > Build Settings.
  2. Select platform and click Switch Platform to activate it.
  3. Confirm Scenes In Build contains desired scenes; put startup scene at index 0.
  4. Set Target Platform options (architecture, compression, development build) and click Build.
Common Mistakes
  • Missing scenes in build list.
  • Building into a protected directory without write permission.
  • Forgetting to switch platform before relying on platform-specific plugins.
Pro Tip

Keep a small validation scene in Scenes In Build for quick sanity checks after switching platforms.

Visual: Build Settings mock
Platforms list

PC, Mac & Linux Standalone, WebGL, Android, iOS. Switch Platform triggers re-import.

Scenes In Build

Drag scenes here or use Add Open Scenes. Ensure startup index is 0 for predictable launch.

Build options

Development Build includes profiler and debug symbols. Uncheck for final releases to reduce overhead.

Checklist before clicking Build
  • Scenes in build and startup index verified.
  • Destination folder exists and is writable.
  • Correct architecture selected (x86 vs x86_64).

screens.title: PC, Mac & Linux Standalone Builds
screens.narratorSegment: Standalone desktop builds are often the simplest to produce but still require attention to options that affect performance and debugging. Desktop targets let you choose the target OS and C P U architecture — for example Windows 64-bit uses x86_64. You must decide whether to build a Development Build during testing; development builds include the Unity Profiler and script debugging symbols so you can attach the profiler or inspect stack traces, but they carry extra overhead and should be unchecked for final releases to optimize performance. A common mistake is leaving the main scene out of the Scenes In Build list so the built executable launches to an empty window or returns to the menu. Another frequent issue is building into a directory without write permissions, which causes the build process to fail late and with confusing errors. Example workflow: select PC, switch platform, pick x86_64, uncheck Development Build for release, and choose a clearly named Build_Windows folder outside the project. Misconception to avoid: development builds are not just slower — they expose debugging hooks and larger file size; treat them as temporary test artifacts. Final question: when would you intentionally use a development build for a player test?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › PC, Mac & Linux Standalone
Options
Target OS & Architecture

Choose Windows, macOS, or Linux and select x86 or x86_64 depending on supported CPUs.

Development Build

Include profiler and debugging symbols while testing. Uncheck for final release to reduce overhead and improve performance.

Pitfalls
  • Forgotten scenes in build list.
  • Building into read-only or protected folders.
  • Relying on editor-only code that won’t run in build.
Concrete Example: Windows release build
  1. Select PC, Mac & Linux Standalone and click Switch Platform.
  2. Under Target Platform choose Windows and Architecture x86_64.
  3. Uncheck Development Build and click Build. Choose a folder named Build_Windows outside Assets.
  4. Run the produced .exe to verify startup and gameplay.
Key Takeaway

Desktop builds are predictable when scenes, architecture, and build destination are verified ahead of time.

screens.title: WebGL Builds and Their Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: WebGL builds convert your Unity project into JavaScript and WebAssembly so it can run inside a browser. This makes your game widely accessible but introduces constraints you don’t encounter on desktop. Web builds are often larger and can suffer slower load times; choosing the right compression format such as Brotli helps reduce download size. Browser security policies can limit features: certain file input and output, synchronous network calls, or native plugin APIs may not be available. Memory is another concern — browsers cap memory more strictly than native runtimes, so large textures or many simultaneous assets can trigger out-of-memory errors. Always test WebGL builds across multiple browsers because performance and supported APIs vary. A practical step is to serve the build with a local web server instead of opening index. html directly; some features require HTTP. Common mistake: not testing the build in the browser's developer console where JavaScript errors appear. Example: a shader or plugin that works in the Editor may fail in WebGL; detect this by inspecting the browser console. Final question: how would you reduce memory usage for a WebGL deployment?

keyIdea.title: WebGL highlights
keyIdea.text: WebGL compiles to JavaScript and WebAssembly, needs compression to reduce download size, and requires careful testing for memory and API limitations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › WebGL Builds
WebGL specifics

WebGL builds output JavaScript and WebAssembly. Choose compression (Brotli recommended for size) and test in modern browsers because runtime behavior can differ.

Compression

Brotli reduces file size and speeds downloads; ensure server supports the compression format you select.

Memory limits

Browsers limit memory; large assets cause out-of-memory errors. Optimize textures and reduce simultaneous allocations.

Testing tip

Serve the build via a local web server for accurate behavior. Opening index.html directly can bypass necessary HTTP behaviors.

Concrete Example

Select WebGL, switch platform, choose Brotli compression, build into Build_WebGL, then serve using a simple local server to open index.html and monitor the browser console for errors.

Common Issues
  • Out-of-memory due to large assets.
  • Unsupported plugins or system calls in browser.
  • JavaScript errors visible only in developer console.
Check Your Understanding

Which two strategies would you use to lower memory usage for WebGL: reduce texture sizes, or split scenes and load additively?

screens.title: Mobile Builds: Android Toolchain
screens.narratorSegment: Android builds require external tools outside of Unity. Android Studio provides the Android SDK, NDK, and an OpenJDK distribution that Unity needs to compile and link native code and packages. In Unity, open Edit, Project Settings, External Tools to point Unity at those installs — specify the SDK path, the NDK path, and the Java Development Kit if Unity does not pick them up automatically. If these paths are incorrect or the required versions are missing, Unity will not produce an Android package. Common mistakes include mismatched NDK versions, missing OpenJDK, or leaving the paths unset. Example workflow: install Android Studio, note the SDK and NDK install locations, configure Unity’s External Tools, then open Build Settings, switch to Android, check Player Settings for the package name and minimum A P I level, and click Build. Also be mindful of signing for publishing: debug keys let you install on devices during testing, but release keys are required for store distribution. Misconception: Unity will not always auto-configure everything; verify paths explicitly. Closing question: what would you check first if an Android build immediately fails before compile?

keyIdea.title: Android toolchain
keyIdea.text: You must install Android Studio and configure Unity’s External Tools with the SDK, NDK, and JDK paths to enable Android builds.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Android Toolchain
Prerequisites
  • Install Android Studio to get Android SDK and NDK.
  • Confirm OpenJDK availability or install a compatible JDK.
  • Note install paths to set in Unity’s External Tools.
External Tools configuration

In Unity: Edit > Project Settings > External Tools. Enter SDK, NDK, and JDK paths or let Unity use embedded versions when available.

Common mistakes

Wrong NDK versions, missing JDK, or leaving paths blank. These usually cause immediate build failures before compilation.

Concrete Example

After installing Android Studio, open Unity External Tools and set the SDK path to Android Studio’s SDK folder. Switch Build Settings to Android and verify Player Settings bundle identifier and minimum API level before building an APK or AAB.

Why it matters

Without proper SDK/NDK/JDK setup, Unity cannot compile native code or produce installable packages for Android devices.

screens.title: Mobile Builds: iOS Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: iOS builds require a Mac O S toolchain and Xcode to compile, sign, and package the application. Unity produces an Xcode project for the iOS target; you open that project in Xcode to perform final signing and export steps. Important Player Settings include the Bundle Identifier — a unique application ID like com. yourcompany. yourgamename — and minimum iOS version to target. Signing is a common friction point: you need provisioning profiles, a valid developer certificate, and correct team settings in Xcode to install on devices or distribute through the App Store. A usual mistake is an incorrect bundle identifier or missing provisioning profile, which prevents installation on physical devices. Example workflow: in Unity set the bundle identifier and target iOS version, switch platform to iOS, build to export an Xcode project, then open Xcode, select a signing team, and run on a connected device. Misconception: Unity does not replace Xcode for iOS — Unity hands off a project to Xcode which must complete the final native compilation and signing. Takeaway: plan Mac O S/Xcode access early when aiming to publish on iOS.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › iOS Requirements
Key steps
  • Set bundle identifier and minimum iOS version in Player Settings.
  • Switch Build Settings to iOS and build to export an Xcode project.
  • Open the exported project in Xcode to set signing and provisioning.
Common pitfalls

Incorrect bundle identifier, missing provisioning profile, or wrong team in Xcode prevent device installs and distribution.

Concrete Example

Set com.company.game in Player Settings, build from Unity to an Xcode project, open the project, choose your signing team, and run on a device connected to your Mac for testing.

Why it matters

iOS builds cannot be completed without Xcode; signing and provisioning are necessary to install and distribute apps.

screens.title: Player Settings and Build Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Player Settings control application-level details that the store platforms and runtime depend on. Important fields include the Bundle Identifier used by stores and device OS to uniquely identify your app, the minimum A P I level which determines the oldest OS version your game supports, and target device types for mobile builds. For WebGL and desktop you also set options like compression format or default screen resolution. The architecture and scripting backend choices influence binary size and compatibility. A common error is an incorrect bundle identifier that conflicts with existing apps or causes signing failures. Another frequent oversight is setting a minimum A P I level that excludes the devices you wish to support. Example: for Android, you may choose a minimum A P I level that balances feature availability and device reach; raising the level can enable newer APIs but reduces installable devices. For production builds, update version numbers and app icons in Player Settings before building and confirm your signing credentials are correct for mobile exports. Takeaway: treat Player Settings as your app's metadata and verify them as part of a pre-release checklist.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Player Settings
Metadata

Company and Product Name, Version, and Bundle Identifier. Update these before release so stores and devices recognize your app correctly.

Targeting

Minimum API level, target architectures, and device types determine compatibility and available APIs at runtime.

Key Takeaway

Player Settings are essential to correct distribution and runtime behavior. Verify them in your release checklist.

Concrete Example

Set com.yourcompany.gamename as the bundle ID, choose a sensible minimum API level for Android, and confirm icons and version numbers before building a release package.

Common Mistake

Forgetting to update version or bundle ID, causing store rejections or conflicts with existing app IDs.

screens.title: Conditional Compilation in C#
screens.narratorSegment: Conditional compilation uses preprocessor directives so you can include or exclude code blocks depending on the build target. This avoids maintaining separate files for each platform and prevents platform-specific APIs from causing compile errors on other targets. For example, you can check UNITY_STANDALONE for desktop input, UNITY_ANDROID or UNITY_IOS for touch input, and UNITY_WEBGL for web-specific behavior. The key benefit is that only the relevant code for the selected platform is compiled into the final build, keeping binaries smaller and preventing A P I misuse. A common misconception is that these directives change behavior at runtime; they actually control compile-time inclusion, so code excluded by a directive is not present in the resulting assembly. Concrete example: a single PlatformSpecificInput script can log mouse clicks on desktop, touch input on mobile, and special handling in WebGL. Always test each conditional branch on its real target: the Editor may simulate standalone behavior but won’t substitute for an actual WebGL browser environment or a physical mobile device. Takeaway: conditional compilation simplifies cross-platform code management but requires testing on each platform to validate behavior.

keyIdea.title: Conditional compilation
keyIdea.text: Use preprocessor directives like #if UNITY_ANDROID to compile platform-specific blocks only when building for those targets.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Conditional Compilation
Concept

Preprocessor directives control which code is compiled for a given build target. Use them to include device-specific input or API calls only where supported.

When to use
  • Different input models (mouse vs touch).
  • Platform-only APIs, such as native sharing or notifications.
  • Optimize binary size by excluding unused platform code.
Key Takeaway

Conditional compilation removes platform-incompatible code from builds and keeps a single codebase manageable across targets.

Concrete code example
using UnityEngine;

public class PlatformSpecificInput : MonoBehaviour
{
  void Update()
  {
#if UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN || UNITY_STANDALONE_OSX
    if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0))
    {
      Debug.Log("Desktop mouse click detected!");
    }
#elif UNITY_ANDROID || UNITY_IOS
    if (Input.touchCount > 0 && Input.GetTouch(0).phase == TouchPhase.Began)
    {
      Debug.Log("Mobile touch detected!");
    }
#elif UNITY_WEBGL
    if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0))
    {
      Debug.Log("WebGL mouse click detected!");
    }
#else
    Debug.Log("Unknown platform input.");
#endif
  }
}
Note: angle brackets and ampersands are escaped for HTML display.
Testing reminder

Compile and run each branch on its target. The Editor can mimic some behavior but does not replace device or browser testing.

screens.title: Testing and Debugging Builds
screens.narratorSegment: Testing builds means validating both runtime behavior and platform integration. Development Build is a Unity build option that includes debug symbols and the Unity Profiler so you can gather frame-by-frame performance data and readable stack traces. Use Development Build when you need to profile or diagnose crashes, but uncheck it for production to remove debugging overhead. For WebGL, open the browser developer console to inspect JavaScript errors generated by the WebAssembly or script glue code; browser logs are often where you’ll find runtime conversion or memory errors. For mobile, check device logs and Xcode or Android logcat output when diagnosing installation or runtime failures. Common resolution steps include verifying Scenes In Build, checking Player Settings for correct bundle IDs and A P I levels, and confirming SDK paths for mobile toolchains. Example troubleshooting flow: if a WebGL build shows a blank page, open the developer console to check for JavaScript exceptions, then test with reduced asset sizes to rule out memory problems. Takeaway: adapt your debugging tools to the platform — profiler and Editor for C P U/memory hotspots, browser console for WebGL errors, and device logs for mobile issues.

keyIdea.title: Debugging builds
keyIdea.text: Use Development Build for profiling and debug symbols; inspect browser console for WebGL and use device logs for mobile.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Testing & Debugging
Development Build

Include profiler and debug symbols for post-build analysis. Use it when diagnosing performance or crashes, but uncheck for final release.

Platform-specific logs
  • WebGL: use browser developer console to inspect JavaScript and memory errors.
  • Android: use logcat to view runtime logs and stack traces.
  • iOS: use Xcode device logs and console output for troubleshooting.
Key Takeaway

Choose the right tool for the platform: profiler for performance, browser console for WebGL, and device logs for mobile errors.

Concrete troubleshooting flow
  1. Run a Development Build and attach the profiler for slow frames.
  2. Inspect logs: browser console for WebGL, logcat for Android, Xcode for iOS.
  3. Reduce assets or tweak compression if memory errors appear.
Common mistake

Relying solely on the Editor to find runtime issues instead of testing on the target platform where APIs and limits differ.

screens.title: Lab: Build Windows then WebGL
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walkthrough guides you to build for Windows and then for WebGL using a small validation scene. Start by opening File, Build Settings and confirm your test scene is in Scenes In Build at index zero. Switch platform to PC, Mac & Linux Standalone, set Target Platform to Windows and Architecture to x86_64. Uncheck Development Build for a release-style test, choose an empty folder named Build_Windows outside your Assets folder, and click Build. After the build completes, run the produced executable to verify startup and basic gameplay. Next, return to Build Settings, choose WebGL, and click Switch Platform — allow Unity time to re-import assets. In WebGL Player Settings select Brotli compression for smaller builds and click Build into Build_WebGL. Serve the generated index. html with a simple local web server to avoid file protocol limitations and open it in a modern browser. Monitor the browser’s developer console for JavaScript or memory errors. For the mini-quiz: what is the purpose of Development Build? Correct answer: it includes profiler and debugging symbols enabling post-build analysis and stack traces; it should be used for testing, not final releases. End by reflecting: which platform revealed the most integration surprises during your build?

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Practice building a Windows executable and a WebGL deployment, and learn when to use Development Build for debugging.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Step-by-step
  1. Open File > Build Settings. Add your validation scene and ensure it is index 0.
  2. Switch to PC, Mac & Linux Standalone. Set Windows target and x86_64. Build to Build_Windows.
  3. Run the produced executable and verify startup and basic interactions.
  4. Switch to WebGL. Choose Brotli compression. Build to Build_WebGL and serve index.html via a local server.
  5. Open the browser console to inspect JavaScript logs and memory usage.
Mini-Quiz

Question: What is the purpose of Development Build? Answer: It includes profiler and debugging symbols for post-build analysis; use it for testing, not for production releases.

Checklist
  • Scenes in build and startup index verified.
  • Correct architecture and compression selected.
  • Destination folders outside Assets and writable.
  • SDK and signing settings configured for mobile if relevant.
Lab Reflection

After building, note errors you saw in Console or browser logs and add a fix to your pre-build checklist for the next iteration.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. First, the Build Process is a staged compilation and packaging workflow that produces platform-specific output. Second, Build Settings is the central Unity window where you select target platforms, add scenes to the build, and choose options like development builds and architecture. Third, Development Build is a testing mode that includes profiling and debugging symbols to help diagnose issues but should be disabled for final releases to optimize performance. Keep these three ideas in mind as you prepare and test each platform build. Key Concepts means treat building as a careful, platform-aware process: configure, test, and validate on the real target.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what it means to build a Unity project for different platforms and why that process is more than just clicking Build. Building compiles your scenes, assets, and scripts into an application package tailored for Windows, WebGL, Android, iOS, and other targets. You will see the key settings that control architecture, development instrumentation, and compression, and you’ll learn the extra toolchain steps required for mobile development. We’ll also walk through platform-specific code using conditional compilation so a single script can behave differently on desktop, mobile, and web. Understanding these stages helps you avoid common mistakes like missing scenes in the build list, wrong SDK paths, or forgetting to uncheck development builds for release. By the end of this chapter you should be able to prepare a simple project, switch targets in Build Settings, configure platform-specific options, and apply a testing plan to verify each build. Think about which platform you’ll ship first and what testing constraints you’ll need — that choice guides many of the configuration decisions you’ll make.

This first set of objectives focuses on understanding the build pipeline and configuring core platform settings. You will learn to describe the build process: what Unity compiles and why the build is platform-specific. Next, you will be able to open and use File, Build Settings to select a target platform, switch platforms, and explain the cost of switching in terms of asset re-imports. You will also learn to configure PC, Mac & Linux Standalone options such as target OS and architecture, and to choose development versus release builds and explain when each is appropriate. Finally, you will study WebGL-specific settings, including compression options and the trade-offs that affect file size and browser performance. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the tangible action you must take during a build. Achieving these skills helps you produce builds that run where you expect and avoid avoidable rework from incorrect settings.

This second set of objectives emphasizes platform-specific code and mobile prerequisites plus deployment testing. You will learn to implement conditional compilation in C#, using preprocessor directives to include or exclude code for desktop, mobile, or WebGL. This technique lets one script adapt to input models, native APIs, or performance characteristics across platforms. You will also learn to configure external tools for mobile builds: specify Android SDK, NDK, and Java paths in Unity’s External Tools, and understand the role of Xcode and signing for iOS builds. Finally, you will practice producing release builds, testing the executable on Windows, and deploying a WebGL build to be opened by a browser or served locally. Each objective explains why the step matters so you can avoid errors like incorrect bundle identifiers or missing SDK versions, and gives a short mnemonic to anchor the competency milestone.

Building in Unity means transforming your project — scenes, assets, and scripts — into a platform-specific package that can run outside the Editor. The build pipeline performs several stages: it first collects the scenes listed in your build, then compiles managed code, processes and compresses assets for the target platform, and finally produces an executable bundle or web deployment package. A key point is that this is not a one-size-fits-all step. Different targets require different output formats, C P U architectures, and runtime support. For example, a Windows build produces an executable and a data folder, while WebGL produces JavaScript and WebAssembly files that run inside a browser. Understanding each stage helps you troubleshoot: missing scenes cause an app that launches without gameplay, incorrect scripting backends or A P I calls can fail at compile time, and mismatched SDK paths will stop mobile builds before compilation begins. A common misconception is that building only packages files — in reality it often reimports assets and can change compression or shader variants for a platform. Example: switching to WebGL can increase import time because textures and audio may be recompressed. Takeaway: treat the build as a staged compilation and test early with small scenes to confirm each stage works as expected. What small scene could you build first to validate your toolchain?

File, Build Settings is the control center for choosing where your game will run. When you open it, you’ll see a list of available platforms such as PC, Mac & Linux Standalone, WebGL, Android, and iOS. Select a platform and click Switch Platform to make it active. Be aware that switching triggers a re-import for many assets, so it can take time. The Scenes In Build list determines which scenes Unity packages; always ensure your main menu or launcher scene is at index zero so startup ordering is predictable. If your build fails immediately after switching, check the Console for script compile errors and verify that platform-specific plugins are compatible. Practical tip: avoid frequent platform switching during active development — pick a primary target and only switch when you’re ready to test another platform. Example workflow: add your test scene to Scenes In Build, switch to Windows Standalone, choose x86_64, deselect Development Build for production, and then click Build to select a destination folder with write permissions. Watch for permission errors when saving into system-protected folders. What step would you add to a pre-build checklist to catch common errors?

Standalone desktop builds are often the simplest to produce but still require attention to options that affect performance and debugging. Desktop targets let you choose the target OS and C P U architecture — for example Windows 64-bit uses x86_64. You must decide whether to build a Development Build during testing; development builds include the Unity Profiler and script debugging symbols so you can attach the profiler or inspect stack traces, but they carry extra overhead and should be unchecked for final releases to optimize performance. A common mistake is leaving the main scene out of the Scenes In Build list so the built executable launches to an empty window or returns to the menu. Another frequent issue is building into a directory without write permissions, which causes the build process to fail late and with confusing errors. Example workflow: select PC, switch platform, pick x86_64, uncheck Development Build for release, and choose a clearly named Build_Windows folder outside the project. Misconception to avoid: development builds are not just slower — they expose debugging hooks and larger file size; treat them as temporary test artifacts. Final question: when would you intentionally use a development build for a player test?

WebGL builds convert your Unity project into JavaScript and WebAssembly so it can run inside a browser. This makes your game widely accessible but introduces constraints you don’t encounter on desktop. Web builds are often larger and can suffer slower load times; choosing the right compression format such as Brotli helps reduce download size. Browser security policies can limit features: certain file input and output, synchronous network calls, or native plugin APIs may not be available. Memory is another concern — browsers cap memory more strictly than native runtimes, so large textures or many simultaneous assets can trigger out-of-memory errors. Always test WebGL builds across multiple browsers because performance and supported APIs vary. A practical step is to serve the build with a local web server instead of opening index. html directly; some features require HTTP. Common mistake: not testing the build in the browser's developer console where JavaScript errors appear. Example: a shader or plugin that works in the Editor may fail in WebGL; detect this by inspecting the browser console. Final question: how would you reduce memory usage for a WebGL deployment?

Android builds require external tools outside of Unity. Android Studio provides the Android SDK, NDK, and an OpenJDK distribution that Unity needs to compile and link native code and packages. In Unity, open Edit, Project Settings, External Tools to point Unity at those installs — specify the SDK path, the NDK path, and the Java Development Kit if Unity does not pick them up automatically. If these paths are incorrect or the required versions are missing, Unity will not produce an Android package. Common mistakes include mismatched NDK versions, missing OpenJDK, or leaving the paths unset. Example workflow: install Android Studio, note the SDK and NDK install locations, configure Unity’s External Tools, then open Build Settings, switch to Android, check Player Settings for the package name and minimum A P I level, and click Build. Also be mindful of signing for publishing: debug keys let you install on devices during testing, but release keys are required for store distribution. Misconception: Unity will not always auto-configure everything; verify paths explicitly. Closing question: what would you check first if an Android build immediately fails before compile?

iOS builds require a Mac O S toolchain and Xcode to compile, sign, and package the application. Unity produces an Xcode project for the iOS target; you open that project in Xcode to perform final signing and export steps. Important Player Settings include the Bundle Identifier — a unique application ID like com. yourcompany. yourgamename — and minimum iOS version to target. Signing is a common friction point: you need provisioning profiles, a valid developer certificate, and correct team settings in Xcode to install on devices or distribute through the App Store. A usual mistake is an incorrect bundle identifier or missing provisioning profile, which prevents installation on physical devices. Example workflow: in Unity set the bundle identifier and target iOS version, switch platform to iOS, build to export an Xcode project, then open Xcode, select a signing team, and run on a connected device. Misconception: Unity does not replace Xcode for iOS — Unity hands off a project to Xcode which must complete the final native compilation and signing. Takeaway: plan Mac O S/Xcode access early when aiming to publish on iOS.

Player Settings control application-level details that the store platforms and runtime depend on. Important fields include the Bundle Identifier used by stores and device OS to uniquely identify your app, the minimum A P I level which determines the oldest OS version your game supports, and target device types for mobile builds. For WebGL and desktop you also set options like compression format or default screen resolution. The architecture and scripting backend choices influence binary size and compatibility. A common error is an incorrect bundle identifier that conflicts with existing apps or causes signing failures. Another frequent oversight is setting a minimum A P I level that excludes the devices you wish to support. Example: for Android, you may choose a minimum A P I level that balances feature availability and device reach; raising the level can enable newer APIs but reduces installable devices. For production builds, update version numbers and app icons in Player Settings before building and confirm your signing credentials are correct for mobile exports. Takeaway: treat Player Settings as your app's metadata and verify them as part of a pre-release checklist.
